summary: Request: isolate webhook callback traffic from long-poll SSE to prevent 429s during peak backfill
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports sustained 429s on production for mixed workflows where webhook callbacks (short HTTP POSTs) coincide with a large long-poll SSE workload used for UI presence updates. They believe health-check probes and short callback bursts are being counted against their tenant burst pool and are exhausting tokens during nightly backfills.

Impact: Intermittent 429s for webhook endpoints (callbacks fail, downstream systems see delayed processing) and sporadic client timeouts for SSE consumers. Business impact: delayed webhooks cause missed metering events and degraded UX for customers during the nightly backfill window.

Timeline:
- 2026-03-09 23:00 UTC: ByteFarms begins scheduled backfill (orchestrator spikes SSE connections).
- 2026-03-10 00:05 UTC: First 429s observed for webhook callback endpoint.
- 2026-03-10 00:20 UTC: Customer opens support ticket after retries do not clear 429s.

Environment: prod-us-east on Dedicated pool (tenant_id: BF-10982). Configuration notes provided by customer: single API key used for both SSE and webhook callback requests; ingress via customer-managed proxy -> Redwood edge; Kubernetes readiness/liveness probes to a /health endpoint on the same domain.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1. Start large-scale SSE clients (10k concurrent long-poll connections) that maintain frequent keepalive pings (every 25s).
2. Trigger a batch backfill that emits ~15k webhook callbacks over 10 minutes using the same API key/tenant.
3. Observe HTTP 429 responses from Redwood for webhook POSTs and occasional truncated SSE reconnects.

Observed behaviour: 429s on webhook POSTs with response header X-RateLimit-Reason: tenant_burst_exhausted. Console shows burst credits consumed rapidly; token refill events are visible but not fast enough to prevent rejections. Customer reports health probes and a set of telemetry beacons that run every 30s also correlate with quota depletion spikes.

Expected behaviour: Short webhook callbacks and health probes should be isolated into a separate short-burst pool or exempted from tenant long-tail credits so that long-lived SSE connections don't starve webhooks during scheduled backfills.

Attachments: request logs (sample), edge gateway timestamps, and a short HAR from a failing webhook POST (provided as links in ticket attachments).
comments: 2026-03-10 00:45 - Priya Patel (Support): Thanks for the details — assigning to Infra/SRE to validate burst accounting and route separation. Can you attach a sample failing request ID if available?

2026-03-10 01:10 - Marcus Lee (SRE): Got the sample logs (req id edge: bf-req-20260310-7a2). Initial glance shows correlated token drain during 00:02-00:08 UTC window. Will pull rate-limiter metrics and refill traces from the dedicated pool.

2026-03-10 02:05 - ByteFarms (Customer): Request IDs: bf-req-20260310-7a2, bf-req-20260310-7b9. Also attached kube readiness probe logs. We suspect our readiness probe hits on /health are being counted and would like them excluded if possible.

2026-03-11 09:20 - Marcus Lee (SRE): Reproduced locally using a scaled SSE simulator. Hypothesis: long-lived SSE keepalive pings are being attributed as interactive tokens against the tenant burst bucket because of shared API-key route. Proposing two options: (1) create route-level separation (route tag) for webhook callback path to map it to an isolated burst pool; (2) create a rule to ignore requests from a health-check IP range (requires team approval for exemptions).

2026-03-12 14:12 - Priya Patel (Support): Proposed config change documented below; scheduled a migration window with customer for 2026-03-13 02:00 UTC. Customer approved route-level separation option.
investigation_notes:
Pulled rate-limiter telemetry for tenant BF-10982: saw burst token count drop from 750 -> 0 between 00:02 and 00:07 UTC while refill continued at configured 60 tokens/min.
Metric links: https://metrics.redwood.com/tenants/BF-10982/burst-tokens?from=2026-03-09T23:50Z&to=2026-03-10T00:20Z
Edge logs show 11k concurrent SSEs during the window. Keepalive frequency 25s causes ~440 keepalive requests/sec aggregated (each counted as a request event).
Health checks: kube readiness probes hitting /health every 15s from node IP pool (~50 nodes) generated an extra ~3-4 requests/sec which contributed to token drain under peak.

Verified current tenant configuration: single default route and single burst pool with smoothing enabled. No route-level pool overrides are configured. Config stored in repo: infra/tenants/BF-10982/config.yaml (PR needed to add route mapping).

Risk assessment: Exempting probes at the edge increases risk of accidental abuse by allowing unauthenticated hits to avoid quota; prefer route-level isolation using authenticated webhook callback path.
resolution:
Workaround applied: created a dedicated route tag /webhook/callback mapped to an isolated short-burst pool with higher refill rate and lower per-request weight; updated tenant BF-10982 routing config and rolled out a canary to 5% of edge nodes at 2026-03-12 03:10 UTC. Result: webhook POST success rate increased to 99.8% during a synthetic backfill test. Follow-ups: (1) customer to rotate API keys used by SSE clients and webhook sender so callbacks map to the new route; (2) SRE to prepare a judgement/PR for probe exemption policy if customer requests it in future.

Notes on fix: Changes made in repo (PR 789) and applied to dedicated pool autoscaler to prevent scale-down during scheduled backfills. Monitored for 48h — no repeat 429s for webhooks during scheduled tests. Ticket resolved with recommended permanent configuration steps documented in Confluence.
follow_up_actions: Customer action: rotate keys for webhook sender and SSE clients as planned (instructions provided).
SRE action: implement a small dashboard to surface route-level burst pool consumption for dedicated tenants (owner: Marcus).
Product action: evaluate a first-class 'health-probe exemption' feature with risk guardrails (owner: Product-Infra).
